sections.title: What Components Contribute to the Mass of an Atom?

slides.title: Mass lives in the nucleus
slides.kicker: Rutherford already told us where the weight sits
bullets: Rutherford's model showed that most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.
Electrons that revolve around the nucleus are so light that their mass can be ignored.
So the story of atomic mass is really the story of the nucleus.
slides.note: Nucleus hi asli weight champion hai!

slides.title: Helium's strange weight
slides.kicker: Two protons, yet four times the mass
bullets: A hydrogen atom has one proton, while a helium atom has two protons.
Yet a helium atom is about four times as heavy as a hydrogen atom, not double.
Early in the 20th century, this mismatch deeply puzzled scientists.

slides.title: The hidden mass suspect
bullets: Scientists wondered whether, besides protons, something else sits in the nucleus.
This mystery particle should add mass without affecting the charge of the atom.
The hunt for a neutral, heavy particle was on.
slides.note: Case file open: the missing mass.

slides.title: Chadwick finds the neutron
bullets: In 1932, James Chadwick, a student of Ernest Rutherford, solved the mass puzzle.
He discovered a subatomic particle with a mass nearly equal to that of a proton but with no electrical charge.
This neutral particle was named the neutron and is represented by the symbol n.

slides.title: Neutrons sit in the nucleus
bullets: Neutrons are found in the nucleus of all atoms except hydrogen.
The mass of an atom comes mainly from its protons and neutrons packed tightly in the nucleus.
This explains why atoms are heavier than the total mass of their protons alone.
slides.note: Hydrogen is the odd one out.

slides.title: Why the nucleus holds
bullets: Every proton inside the nucleus repels every other proton because all carry like positive charges.
Neutral neutrons intervene and increase the distance between protons, reducing this repulsion.
The nuclear force binds all the particles together, so heavier atoms need many more neutrons.
slides.note: Neutrons are the peacekeepers of the nucleus.

slides.title: Neutrons grow with size
slides.kicker: Light atoms match, heavy atoms add more
bullets: Lighter atoms often have equal numbers of protons and neutrons, like carbon with six of each.
Iron has 26 protons and 30 neutrons, already more neutrons than protons.
Uranium's nucleus has 92 protons and 146 neutrons, so heavy atoms carry many more neutrons.

slides.title: India's neutron lab
slides.kicker: Dhruva reactor at work in Mumbai
bullets: The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre in Mumbai leads advanced neutron-scattering experiments using reactors such as Dhruva.
These experiments reveal key insights into superconductors, battery electrodes, and drug molecules.
The neutron's discovery opened a new era in atomic physics: artificial elements and the splitting of uranium atoms.
slides.note: Neutrons even help design better medicines.

slides.title: Dalton draws the first symbols
bullets: John Dalton realised the need for a standard way to represent elements and compounds to make chemistry easier to study.
In 1803 he introduced the first pictorial symbols to represent the known elements.
By 1869 scientists knew 69 elements; today about 118 are known, some made artificially.

slides.title: Berzelius goes alphabetic
bullets: In 1813, Berzelius suggested that symbols of elements should be derived from their Latin names.
This gave alphabetic chemical symbols, the letter style still used today.
These alphabetic symbols replaced Dalton's drawn pictures.

slides.title: IUPAC writes the rules
bullets: The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) approves the names and symbols of elements.
Many symbols are the first letter or the first two letters of the element's name.
The first letter is always uppercase and the second, if present, is lowercase: Al for aluminium, not AL; Co for cobalt, not CO.
Some symbols use the first letter plus a different letter, like Cl for chlorine and Zn for zinc.

slides.title: Symbols from old tongues
slides.kicker: Latin, Greek and German live in chemistry
bullets: Some element symbols come from their Latin, Greek, or German names rather than English.
Iron is Fe from the Latin ferrum, and mercury is Hg from the Greek hydrargyros.
Tungsten is W from the German wolfram.
Scientists use these symbols because they are internationally recognised and cut across language barriers.

slides.title: Z counts the protons
bullets: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom of an element is known as its atomic number.
It is designated by the symbol Z.
Z determines the identity of an element and its chemical behaviour.

slides.title: Neutral means balanced
bullets: Since the atom as a whole is neutral, its number of protons equals the number of electrons orbiting the nucleus.
Hydrogen has one proton and one electron, so its atomic number is 1.
Helium, with atomic number 2, has 2 protons and 2 electrons.

slides.title: Z is the identity card
slides.kicker: No two elements share a Z
bullets: Atoms of an element are all alike, but differ from the atoms of other elements in their protons and electrons.
Elements with different atomic numbers are distinct from each other.
So the atomic number uniquely identifies an element, like an identity card.

items: That count is the atomic number Z
Z fixes the element's identity and behaviour

slides.title: Count every particle
slides.kicker: From Z and A to the full roster
bullets: Z directly gives the protons, and in a neutral atom the electrons equal the protons.
Subtract Z from the total number of nucleons to get the neutrons.
Example: an atom with atomic number 26 and 56 nucleons has 26 protons, 26 electrons, and 30 neutrons.

items: Electrons = Z for a neutral atom

slides.title: A adds protons and neutrons
slides.kicker: The nucleus weighs in as one number
bullets: The total number of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus of an atom is called its mass number, denoted by A.
The protons and neutrons present in the nucleus are together called nucleons.
Mass number = Number of protons + Number of neutrons.

slides.title: Helium's mass explained
bullets: The mass of a neutron is roughly equal to that of a proton.
So the mass of a helium atom is accounted for by two protons and two neutrons.
The electron, in comparison, has almost negligible mass and is ignored in calculations.

items: Mass works out to about 4 proton masses

slides.title: Standard notation
slides.kicker: A on top, Z below, symbol aside
bullets: In the standard notation for an atom, the symbol is written along with its atomic number Z and mass number A.
The mass number A goes at the top left and the atomic number Z at the bottom left of the element's symbol.
Carbon has atomic number 6 and mass number 12, written as 12 over 6 C.

slides.title: Next: the electron map
bullets: Protons and neutrons are located in the nucleus of an atom, while electrons move around the nucleus.
The next question is how these electrons are arranged around the nucleus.
Bohr and Bury's shell rules, with shells K, L, M and N, answer this in the coming sections.

items: They arrange in shells K, L, M, N

slides.note: Ab electrons ke ghar ginte hain.

examples.title: Solving the helium mass puzzle
examples.problem: A helium atom has two protons, yet its mass is about four times that of a hydrogen atom. Using the neutron, explain where the extra mass comes from.
steps: Rutherford's model says atomic mass sits almost entirely in the nucleus.
Helium's nucleus has 2 protons, contributing the mass of 2 protons.
Helium's mass is about 4 proton masses, so about 2 units of mass are still missing.
Chadwick's neutron has a mass nearly equal to a proton and no charge, so 2 neutrons fill the gap without changing helium's charge.
examples.answer: Helium's mass is accounted for by 2 protons and 2 neutrons packed in its nucleus.

examples.title: Identifying an atom from its numbers
examples.problem: An atom has atomic number 26 and 56 nucleons in its nucleus. Find its number of protons, electrons and neutrons, and name the element using the chapter's data.
steps: The atomic number Z equals the number of protons, so protons = 26.
The atom is neutral, so electrons = protons = 26.
Nucleons are protons plus neutrons, so neutrons = 56 - 26 = 30.
The chapter notes that iron has 26 protons and 30 neutrons, so this atom is iron.
examples.answer: 26 protons, 26 electrons and 30 neutrons; the atom is iron (Fe).

examples.title: Writing standard notation for carbon
examples.problem: Carbon's atomic number is 6 and its mass number is 12. Write carbon in standard notation and state how many neutrons it has.
steps: Place the mass number A = 12 at the top left of the symbol.
Place the atomic number Z = 6 at the bottom left of the symbol.
Neutrons = A - Z = 12 - 6 = 6, so carbon has 6 protons and 6 neutrons.
examples.answer: Carbon is written as 12 over 6 C, with 6 protons and 6 neutrons in its nucleus.
